speaker: Jonathan Gray
title: Blackstone's Jon Gray on real estate, rates, and building a winning company culture
question: In leveraged buyouts and M&A, how does a shift to falling interest rates mechanically restart frozen deal activity?
guest: To sort of understand real-world why this matters to transactions, we did a deal with Emerson. When we tried to do that, we could borrow at 13%. That was basically the cost of debt capital, and we could only borrow in the markets 20 or 25% of the total enterprise. Think about the cost of capital when you weigh in equity as well at high teens. That makes doing deals very hard. So as the Fed lowers rates, as the 10-year Treasury comes down, people become more interested in fixed income, spreads start to tighten there, and the weighted average cost of capital comes way down. And that starts to get that flywheel going. Now, the other piece of this is the IPO market, which should restart. As equities continue to rally, that will be like a magnet sucking in private companies. Yes, the early ones will come out at bigger discounts, but you'll begin to see more transaction activity. If you went back to the early nineties or after the financial crisis, M&A volume fell 50, 60%, and then it started to rebuild.

points.core: Tight credit markets severely cap how much debt buyers can borrow per deal.
points.note: Accept: restricted leverage availability (e.g., borrowing only 20–25% of enterprise value) forces more expensive equity into the capital stack, making buyout math unworkable. Do not credit: merely saying high interest rates make debt expensive.

points.core: Falling benchmark rates draw capital into fixed income, compressing credit spreads.
points.note: Accept: declining policy rates or Treasury yields spur investor demand for credit, narrowing risk spreads on top of lower base rates. Do not credit: merely stating lower rates reduce borrowing costs without mentioning spread compression.

points.core: Lower weighted average cost of capital restores deal math across buyout markets.
points.note: Accept: blended debt-and-equity financing costs falling enough to close bid-ask spreads and revive M&A volume. Do not credit: vague claims that lower rates boost general market confidence.

points.core: Rallying public equities act as a magnet pulling private companies toward IPOs.
points.note: Accept: rising stock valuations reopen the IPO window, drawing private companies back to public listings (often starting at wider discounts). Do not credit: generic mentions of improved investor sentiment without linking equity rallies to IPO reopening.

models.label: Claude Fable 5.2
models.answer:
Falling rates restart deals mainly by repairing the financing math and closing the gap between what buyers can pay and what sellers will accept.

In an LBO, the purchase price is largely funded with floating-rate debt, so the amount a target can borrow is capped by how much interest its cash flow can cover. When rates drop, the same EBITDA supports more debt at the same coverage ratio, so sponsors can pay a higher price while still hitting their target returns. Lower rates also reduce discount rates, lifting valuations generally.

That matters because deal freezes are usually a bid-ask standoff: sellers anchor to prices from the cheap-money era, while buyers facing expensive debt can't meet them. Cheaper leverage raises buyers' bids toward sellers' expectations, and the spread closes.

Supporting mechanics reinforce this. Credit markets reopen as lenders and CLO investors regain appetite, so banks will underwrite and syndicate debt again. Existing portfolio companies get interest relief and can refinance, making them saleable. Exits then return cash to limited partners, which funds new commitments and gives sponsors pressure and capacity to deploy dry powder.

models.label: Gemini Carbon
models.answer: Falling interest rates restart frozen deal activity by expanding buyer purchasing power, closing valuation gaps, and reopening credit and exit markets. In leveraged buyouts, acquisition debt is priced off floating benchmarks or prevailing bond yields; lower rates directly reduce interest expense, improving a target’s interest coverage ratios and allowing lenders to underwrite higher debt-to-EBITDA multiples. With larger, cheaper debt packages available, private equity sponsors can pay higher purchase multiples while still clearing their target internal rate of return hurdles, and strategic acquirers benefit from a lower cost of capital that lifts discounted cash flow valuations. This added buyer capacity bridges the bid-ask spread with sellers anchored to higher historical prices. Simultaneously, falling and stabilizing rates reduce hung-debt risk for underwriting banks, bringing syndicated loan and high-yield bond markets back alongside direct lenders at tighter credit spreads. Finally, lower financing costs let sponsors refinance maturing debt and sell existing portfolio companies to newly funded buyers, returning cash to limited partners and unlocking capital for fresh acquisitions.

models.label: Claude Opus 5.5
models.answer:
When rates fall, deals start up again through a few connected mechanical changes.

The first is debt capacity. LBOs are limited by interest coverage, so cheaper floating-rate debt (SOFR plus a spread) lets the same EBITDA carry more leverage. Sponsors can borrow more and put in less equity, which raises the IRR they can model at a given price.

The second is valuation. A lower discount rate raises the present value of future cash flows and lifts trading multiples. That narrows the gap between what buyers will pay and what sellers expect, which is what froze activity in the first place. Sellers who wouldn't accept lower marks finally see prices they'll take.

The third is financing markets. Leveraged loan and high-yield issuance reopens, banks underwrite again, and CLOs buy the paper. Companies refinance maturing debt, which removes the risk of being forced to sell or restructure.

Exits then free up the rest of the cycle. Higher valuations make IPOs, sales to other sponsors and strategic sales workable, so sponsors can return capital to their investors (LPs). Those LPs then commit to new funds, and record unspent capital ("dry powder") gets put to work. Each completed deal makes the next one easier to price and finance.

models.label: GPT-6.2-Sol
models.answer:
Falling rates can restart deal activity by raising the price buyers can afford to pay. When lower benchmark rates flow through to acquisition loans, the same debt balance costs less to service. In a leveraged buyout, that lets the sponsor borrow more for a given level of cash flow or keep the same debt balance and use the interest savings to pay down principal faster. Either way, the sponsor can bid more while still meeting its target equity return.

Lower discount rates can also raise what future cash flows are worth to buyers, including strategic acquirers. Deals start moving again when those higher bids reach prices sellers will accept. The effect depends on why rates are falling. Wider credit spreads, tighter lending standards, or weaker expected earnings can offset the benefit of a lower benchmark rate.

models.answer:
Falling rates can restart deals by closing the gap between what sellers will accept and what buyers can finance. In a leveraged buyout, if borrowing costs fall, the same amount of debt requires less interest, leaving more of the target’s cash flow available to pay down principal. That raises the buyer’s expected equity return at the old bid price and gives it room to bid more while still meeting its return target. If lenders size the loan around the target’s ability to cover interest, they may also lend more against the same earnings.

For a corporate acquirer, cheaper financing lowers the cost of a debt-funded purchase. Across M&A, lower discount rates can also raise the present value buyers assign to future cash flows and synergies. A stalled deal can move once a buyer’s financeable bid meets the seller’s price. That depends on actual borrowing costs falling and earnings holding up. Wider credit spreads or weaker cash flows can offset a rate cut.
